newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: National ID card system raises ire in Philippines.
newsitem.headline: National ID card system raises ire in Philippines.

text.p: Philippine President Fidel Ramos faced a political tempest on Sunday as human rights groups, politicians and lawyers slammed his order creating a national identification card system, calling it an "Orwellian nightmare".
Critics said it was reminiscent of late president Ferdinand Marcos's attempts to curb dissent while opposition senator Blas Ople warned Ramos could be impeached if he did not revoke his order.
Ramos last week ordered the adoption of a national computerised identification system whereby Filipinos would be issued official identification cards by the government.
The cards, which would bear the carriers' fingerprints, would make it convenient for them to transact business with government and even private offices, officials said.
Use of a national card would "reduce if not totally eliminate fradulent transactions and misrepresentations," the order said.

A human rights committee of the country's main lawyers group, the Intergrated Bar of the Philippines, said the order would pave the way for the creation of "a surveillance system ... to monitor the activities and whereabouts of everybody."
"Surely a private person's fingerprints is not a matter of public interest," it said.
Laban (Fight) opposition party chief Senator Edgardo Angara said Ramos would turn the country "into an Orwellian state."

"The government is laying down the foundation of a country akin to the state described in George Orwell's novel '1984' in which 'big brother' watches over the shoulders of citizens all the time," Angara said. a
Another lawyers group, the Public Interest Law Centre, called for a civil disobedience campaign to stop the government.
"An Orwellian nightmare," the Centre called the move.
Other lawyers said they were considering asking the Supreme Court to annull the presidential order as unconstitutional.
"They are seeing ghosts when there should be none," presidential executive secretary Ruben Torres said on Saturday.
"This is merely for identification so people will not be carrying three, five IDs all the time."
